https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2021/04.title: Owner of horse called Isis flagged as potential terrorist over payment
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2021/04.subtitle: Susan Govindasamy found herself facing a security grilling after making a £500 payment with the reference 'funds for Isis'
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2021/04.text:
The owner of an unfortunately named horse had her online payments frozen and found herself flagged as a potential terrorist after sending a trainer “funds for Isis”.
Susan Govindasamy was hoping to arrange for her nine-year-old Arab horse, called Isis, to attend a training “bootcamp” and agreed to send £500 to cover the costs over PayPal.
The 57-year-old had, however, failed to grasp that the wording of her transfer could have grave security implications.
Her payment was quickly frozen after the reference - “funds for Isis” - was flagged at PayPal, which feared she may have been trying to fund terrorism.
Ms Govindasamy, from Bolton, Greater Manchester, is passionate about Ancient Egypt and named her horse after the Egyptian goddess Isis, rather than the murderous terror cult.
She has previously owned horses called Pharaoh and Nefertiti, both also allusions to Egyptian history.
Three days after agreeing to send the cash, Ms Govindasamy was contacted by the trainer to say nothing had been received - and found the transaction was still pending.
She said she was left “speechless” when she was then contacted by PayPal and told her transaction was under review to “minimise risk for us or our customers”.
The confusion meant she was forced to explain she had been paying for her horse’s training rather than funnelling money to extremists. She was even required to provide her horse’s passport as proof.
Ms Govidasamy claimed she was also contacted by Interpol over the security scare, but the policing organisation does not contact individuals directly and its national bureau in the UK provides intelligence and support to the National Crime Agency (NCA).
She said: "I'm really interested in Ancient Egypt - Isis is the goddess of goddesses.
"When Isis was born, if she'd been a colt he would have been called Osiris. When I knew she was a filly I knew Isis was the name for her.”
After the rise of the terror group, Ms Govidasamy recalled, she had several people tell her that she would “have to change her name”.
"I said 'I'm not changing her name, I absolutely refuse she's called Isis after the Egyptian goddess and if people can't get past that then they've got an issue',” she continued.
The horse owner, who described herself as “a bit scatty”, said the payment wording “went right over my head” until her husband explained why it had been flagged.
“When the penny dropped I was speechless,” she said.
"I'd been flagged as a potential terrorist. I remember thinking 'what does this mean, what will happen now?'.
"I was investigated, as was the other side where the money was going to, and I explained in detail what was happening and that my horse was called Isis.”
She claimed she had to sign a declaration that she had no connection or affiliation to a terror group of any sort before the funds were finally released.
The horse trainer, who asked not to be named, shared details of the story online, writing: "That embarrassing moment when you get asked a million questions to check if you are a terrorist or not because Susan Govindasamy uses Ice's official name of Isis on a payment reference through PayPal.
"There's me telling him to Google it and it's after a goddess not actually Isis-related oh gosh embarrassing.
"Susan from now on she's Ice especially when sending payment references."
A spokesman for PayPal said Government regulations require that companies which process payments including PayPal scan all transactions for “terrorist and other references”.
They added: "We do everything we can to eliminate references that have nothing to do with terrorism, and work with customers to resolve quickly any issues that might inadvertently arise."

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2021/04.title: Meet Tony Sewell, the man who took on the race clique
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2021/04.subtitle: The educationalist’s controversial report on racism in Britain has left him facing a barrage of abuse, but who is he? Mick Brown reports
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2021/04.text:
This has been a particularly uncomfortable week for Dr Tony Sewell.
On Wednesday, the Commission on Race and Ethnic Disparities, of which Sewell was chairman, issued its report, concluding that factors such as geography, family influence, socio-economic background, culture and religion have more significant impact on life chances than the existence of racism, and that while racism unquestionably exists in some areas, the progress made by ethnic minorities in Britain over the past 50 years “should be regarded as a model for other white-majority countries”.
Cue outrage.
Maurice Mcleod, chief executive of the social policy think tank Race on the Agenda, attacked the 258-page report as “government-level gaslighting”, while Halima Begum, head of the Runnymede Trust, criticised its “cultural deafness”, calling it a “gross offence” to grieving families of ethnic minorities who have died of Covid.
Responding to a passage arguing the need to tell “a new story” about the slave trade effecting a cultural transformation of African people, the shadow equalities minister Marsha De Cordova demanded that the Government “urgently explain” how the report came to publish content “which glorifies the slave trade”.
Sewell later issued a statement saying: “It is absurd to suggest that the commission is trying to downpay the evil of the slave trade. It is both ridiculous and offensive to each and every commissioner.”
Then it got personal.
Tony Sewell has long been, in many ways, a heretic. He has spent his career speaking out against the accepted shibboleths of race relations, and saying “the unsayable” about knife crime and the reasons for underachievement among young black people. He has long been described as an apologist for Tory policies, a man “bought” by the establishment.
But the attacks he has received this week have been on an altogether different order of vitriol. He has been called an “Uncle Tom” and “a coconut”. The Labour MP Clive Davis tweeted an image of the Ku Klux Klan (notwithstanding the fact that nine of the 10 members of the commission are of ethnic minority origin).
Sewell is said to be “shocked”. “He was expecting the report to be received negatively in some quarters and to be criticised, but the abuse has been on a different scale,” says one friend who has worked with him over the years.
Katharine Birbalsingh, the black British educator, co-founder and headmistress of the Michaela Community School in Wembley, and no stranger to insults herself, says: “It’s not Tony they hate so much, it’s what he’s saying.
“The standard Leftist belief is that Britain is a racist country and he’s saying it’s not. But for the Left it is simply unacceptable to question their views. You are a bad person by definition for having an alternative opinion – and this is even more the case if you aren’t white, because black people are meant to toe the line and, if they don’t, then they are traitors and that’s the biggest possible sin.”
Much has been said over the past few days about how the report ignores the “lived experience” of ethnic minorities in Britain. Less about how the lived experience of Sewell himself has weighed in the report.
A tall man of considerable girth, Sewell was born in Brixton in 1959 and grew up in the south London suburb of Penge. His parents were among the Windrush generation who arrived in London in the Fifties from Jamaica. His mother worked in a factory and his father was a car mechanic. Growing up, he once said: ‘“I was strongly influenced by my parents’ Jamaican culture. For me, it was both good and bad. It gave me cultural awareness but it also kept me feeling homeless – I felt that this wasn’t really my space. On the one hand, multiculturalism gives you something but, on the other hand, it can disorientate you away from the place where you are and where you really want to be.”
He has spoken of how he was frequently in trouble as a child, until his mother’s decision to attend a predominantly white Anglican church. Much of his adolescence was spent in church youth-group activities. It was that, he said, that first instilled him with “middle-class values” and the possibility that he might go to university: “No one at my school went to university, but suddenly we were like, ‘I’m going to go to university as well.’”
This sense of bettering yourself has been a recurring theme for Sewell throughout his life.
“He’s always seen obstacles as something to get over, not to stop him,” says one friend.
In 1981, Sewell graduated from the University of Essex where he studied English Literature. He went on to teach in inner-city comprehensives in north and south London, before leaving to teach in Jamaica for two years.
It was a country, he told the BBC in 2008, that he was “ill-prepared for... Probably as ill-prepared as my parents were, when they came from Jamaica to live in London in the Fifties. After two years, I felt there was no future for me there, so I came back.”
He returned to teaching and went on to write a PhD thesis which was published in 1997 under the title Black Masculinities and Schooling: How Black Boys Survive Modern Schooling. A study of an inner-city boys’ comprehensive school, it marked out what would be his abiding preoccupations, with ideas of masculinity and self-perception among black boys, the role of the family in the black community and what he has called “the elephant in the room” of absent fathers, leading black boys to forge their identities through gang culture.
“These boys are like Hamlet, thinking too much about their absent fathers,” he wrote in a Telegraph article in 2018. “This ghost has not been exorcised. They have simply been left looking at their peers, which is like looking in the mirror. They also have a strong right arm, which they all too often put to ill use... A father going AWOL is something akin to post-traumatic stress disorder. When the father is absent or failing in his duty, our boys are left isolated and a danger.”
He has been particularly critical of the stereotyping that he believes underpins so many youth programmes that attempt to divert black boys from crime with “yet another” DJing or football scheme. He once wrote to the London mayor Sadiq Khan suggesting a video campaign showing “black men just being boring”, and pointing out that the “the country’s biggest bird-watching expert is a black boy from Hackney.
“A lot of black men do take care of their child. Let’s see more of them – and more of boys doing maths – instead of having former gang members helping potential gang members make rap videos for YouTube.”
“Tony has spent a lifetime analysing these things and he’s seen them play out in schools and the inner city. It’s a great shame that the Left refuses to listen, because the people who lose out are the very black boys they claim to be trying to help,” Birbalsingh says.
Education as a route out of disadvantage has always been Sewell’s abiding creed. Like Birbalsingh, he is a champion advocate of Academy schools. A former education advisor to Boris Johnson when he was mayor of London, Sewell was part of the team that opened Mossbourne Community Academy in 2004 on the site of Hackney Downs School, which was described as the “worst school in Britain”. In 2011/12 it achieved the distinction of getting seven per cent of its leavers into Oxbridge.
In 2005 Sewell set up Generating Genius, to help (principally black) boys from economically disadvantaged backgrounds to study STEM subjects at top universities. “People ask if we did black studies with these pupils,” he once remarked. “No! We didn’t do any of that. We just did really really difficult science.” According to its website 450 pupils have completed the programme since 2005, 100 per cent have received work-experience related to STEM subjects and graduates have gone on to work for Shell, BP and investment banks.
In 2006 Sewell was awarded a CBE in recognition of his work in education. But not everything he has touched has been a success. Generating Genius was the inspiration for another project initiated by Sewell, the STEM 6th Form Academy, that he was involved in setting up in 2013, at a reported cost of more than £13m. But after two years, and STEM’s first Ofsted report labelling the school inadequate in all categories, it was taken over by Aspirations Academies Trust. The school finally closed in 2019. “Tony’s a very affable and well-meaning guy,” says one person who worked with him in the past, “but I got the sense there was no real leadership there.”
“Ain’t nothing romantic about being working class,” Sewell once said in an interview. “Most working-class people who are genuinely working class want to come out of it. That’s the definition of it. You don’t want to stay in it.”
Sewell’s own ascent up the class ladder can be measured in the journey he has made from inner-city (if nowadays considerably gentrified) Brixton to the leafy suburbs of south Croydon – some 10 miles away – where he now lives.
He has been married to his wife Adele for 30 years. Last year she won an Amazing Woman award from Woman and Home magazine for transforming her ongoing personal battle over 21 years against breast and then ovarian cancer into a successful charity. Her annual event, The Touch of Teal Tea, has raised over £160,000 to date for Ovacome. The couple have a 26-year-old daughter and Sewell has talked of how much better life was for her growing up than it had been for him.
“The biggest difference is being a black child in London now is a lot more positive than it was then. She is never going to face the level of racism – the overt racism – that we did, particularly on the street. She has experienced a couple of racist incidents, but we used to have it night and day. So that is completely different. I’m not saying that it is utopia now, as I’m aware that she is middle class and that she’s insulated from a lot.”
Described by friends as “always cheerful”, Sewell says his hobbies are “looking after my goldfish and sitting in my hammock”. He loves Jamaica and visits every couple of years. Birbalsingh remembers him enthusing after one visit about how he had been helping children to read and understand Shakespeare.
“That’s the kind of thing he gets excited about.
“He doesn’t take things too seriously, and he takes things in his stride,” she says. “But you have to be like that when you take on what he’s done, otherwise you’d get pulled down by all the negativity and the ad hominems sent your way.”
For the moment, the negativity and the ad hominems are at gale force.
“It’s really upsetting when the mob comes for you,” says Birbalsingh. “But my advice to Tony has been, blinkers on, keep your eyes on your goal, come off social media, do not get involved in any arguments, and be around people you love.”
It is advice Sewell seems to be heeding. He is unavailable for comment. But friends say not for long.
“Tony is on a mission,” says one. “He’s an idealist and he wants to make a difference. He won’t be intimidated by any of this. He genuinely believes what he says and thinks and he’s not easily cowed.”

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/fashion/styl.title: Greenwashing: a guide for confused beginners
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/fashion/styl.text:
Ethical shopping should be getting easier, as awareness grows of fashion’s toxic impact and the industry responds to urgent calls to do better. But with everyone keen to hitch a free ride on the sustainability bandwagon, it can be hard to know who to trust.
From premium labels to some of fast fashion’s worst offenders, brands are out to pull the wool over shoppers’ eyes with claims – whether fraudulent, misleading or wildly exaggerated – to persuade us they’re more ethical than they are. Buzzwords like ‘conscious’, ‘eco-friendly’, ‘clean’ and ‘responsible’ can be bandied about freely without stats to back them up, while token gestures can be spun into PR noise that drowns out the truth.
“The reality is that sustainability has become a marketing tool,” admits Orsola de Castro, Founder and Global Creative Director of not-for-profit Fashion Revolution. This week is Fashion Revolution Week, marking eight years since the Rana Plaza garment factory collapse in Bangladesh killed 1,134 workers. This awareness-raising campaign encourages the public to ask the questions 'who made my clothes' and 'what are they really made of'.
de Castro explains that greenwashing takes many forms, but all aim to score points without sacrificing profit. “For some brands it will be environmental, for others social. But it’s generally taking something very small and pretending it’s game-changing when it isn’t.”
A prime example is recycling ‘take-back’ schemes, which we’ve seen in recent years from a slew of retailers including H&M, Primark, Zara and New Look. While anything that keeps old clothes out of the bin is arguably positive, offering incentives like a 10% discount on new products for all those who recycled only urges us to keep on shopping – and the brands show no sign of scaling back their production.
Meanwhile, the technology to recycle clothes into new ones remains limited, which creates a staggering false equivalence. Back in 2016, the journalist Lucy Seigle calculated that it would take a brand like H&M roughly 12 years to recycle the same volume of clothes it produces in 48 hours. The tech may have improved since then, but it is still likely nowhere near enough to offset the volume.
It helps to step back and look at the bigger picture; not just at the one or two ‘hero’ products, but the full scale of a brand’s retail offering. When fast fashion behemoth Boohoo launched its For the Future range boasting clothes made with 95% recycled materials, the greenwashing glowed brighter than kryptonite. Even recycled polyester can take up to 200 years to break down in landfill – which, considering the trend-longevity of the average Boohoo fast fashion item, is where most are likely to end up.
Recently, fans and press were quick to applaud the launch of ASOS’ new Circular Collection. But sustainability activists did the maths. A modest 29-piece collection, the brand’s attempt at circularity comprises just 0.035% of its current stock. The headlines might make waves, but the reality is a drop in the fast fashion ocean.
Fabric can be a greenwashing blind spot too. ‘Natural’ fibres are often touted by brands as a more sustainable option – and it’s certainly true that cotton, linen, wool and hemp all decompose faster than synthetics, and don’t leach microplastic particles into the ocean. But their supply chains can still be laden with chemicals and rife with issues. Non-organic cotton has been dubbed “the world’s dirtiest crop”, thanks to the colossal volumes of water and pesticides used to grow it, and the forced labour still used, in some countries, to pick it.
Viscose, made from wood pulp, is often championed as a ‘plant-based’ solution – yet its intensive manufacture is linked to deforestation, air pollution and water contamination. ‘Vegan’, meanwhile, is often used as a synonym for sustainability, despite the most common faux leathers and synthetic wools being plain ol’ plastic by another name.
Recent times have seen a rise in ‘wokewashing’, greenwashing’s right-on cousin, which uses gestures of inclusivity to deflect attention from behind-the-scenes oppression. A ‘feminist’ t-shirt made for poverty wages by young women in Bangladesh. An ‘empowering’ ad campaign from a brand with an entirely white, male board. Last summer, as black squares flooded social media and brands fell over themselves to shout about equality at the beginning of the Black Lives Matter movement, those same retailers actively withheld billions of pounds from some of the world’s very poorest people of colour. True sustainability needs to be holistic; treating the planet and all of its inhabitants with equal respect.
While writing my book How To Break Up With Fast Fashion, I was reminded time and again of that old lateral thinking puzzle about trying to get a fox, a chicken and a bag of grain in a boat across a river. For every solution, a new problem seemingly arises. For every positive story, there’s a problematic footnote. It can be exhausting for the average shopper to find our efforts at conscious consumerism undermined at every turn, so it’s no surprise that we’re willing to put our trust in brands who talk the talk.
But while some might argue that all good intentions have to begin somewhere, letting this kind of corporate bluffing go unchallenged can bring true progress to a screeching halt.
“Greenwashing derails the quest for knowledge and accuracy, which is incredibly important,” says De Castro. “By making [sustainability] seem overly simplistic, it doesn’t bring the consumer anywhere nearer to understanding the real issues.”
So how do we sort the good from the greenwash? “Customers have to become savvy,” she says, “just as they’re savvy about where to get the biggest discount, or the style that suits them better.” For those who argue that sustainable shopping is too time-consuming but will spend days hunting for the ‘perfect’ dress, it’s a salient point.
Luckily there are tools to help us do our homework. The Good On You brand directory is one of the most useful, with at-a-glance ratings for thousands of fashion brands. Ethical Consumer provides some of the most in-depth analysis around, while Fashion Revolution’s Fashion Transparency Index is a yearly review of the world’s biggest brands and how much they disclose about their supply chain. Transparency doesn’t necessarily equal sustainability – H&M came top of the table this year, amid much controversy – but if a brand is hiding something, there’s probably a reason.
Accreditation can help make things clearer too. Keep an eye out for industry stamps of approval, like the Global Organic Textile Standard (GOTS) or Oeko-Tex for fabrics, Fairwear Foundation for ethical labour practises and B Corp for companies that balance purpose with profit. Sustainably-made TENCEL is a safer bet than viscose or bamboo, while new innovations like piñatex (leather made from pineapple leaves) and Weganool (plant-based wool) are better ways for vegans to go.
When faced with marketing spiel, focus on stats and percentages, and don’t be dazzled by sweeping, grandiose statements. “Look for sensationalism,” warns De Castro. “Anything that says it’s going to save the world, is definitely not.”
Where there are gaps in our knowledge, we can ask questions. The hashtag #WhoMadeMyClothes has been holding fashion accountable since 2013, and whether it’s a tweet, an email or a petition, demanding more information from our favourite brands is one of the most powerful ways shoppers can create change.
Finally, if confusion still abounds, stick to the age-old rule of thumb. If something sounds too good to be true, then it probably is.
